plain_title: Feeling unreal, or like the world is
one_liner: Persistent feelings of being detached from yourself, or of the world being unreal, while knowing it's a feeling.
in_simple_words: Depersonalization is feeling detached from your own body, thoughts, or feelings, as if watching yourself from outside or going through the motions like a robot. Derealization is the world feeling unreal: foggy, flat, dreamlike, or far away. Almost everyone feels this briefly under stress, exhaustion, or after cannabis. The disorder is when it's persistent or keeps returning, causes real distress, and the person knows it's a feeling rather than reality. It's frightening but not dangerous, and it's treatable.
what_it_can_feel_like: It's like there's a pane of glass between me and everything. I can see life. I can't touch it.
I thought I was going insane. The doctor said: the fact you're worried you're insane means you're not.
CBT helped me stop checking whether I felt real every five minutes. That checking was keeping it going.
common_signs: Feeling detached from your body, thoughts, or feelings; watching yourself from outside
The world seeming unreal, dreamlike, foggy, or lifeless
Knowing the feeling isn't reality (intact reality testing)
Persistent or recurring, causing real distress or impairment
Often triggered by anxiety, panic, trauma, or cannabis
Anxiety about the symptoms themselves, which keeps them going

myths_vs_facts.myth: Feeling unreal means you're going mad or becoming psychotic.
myths_vs_facts.fact: In DPDR you know it's a feeling. That's the opposite of psychosis. It's a common anxiety-linked symptom, not a sign of losing your mind.
DPDR often fades on its own and responds to treatment. The fear of it being permanent is one of the things that keeps it going.
Around 1 in 100 people has the disorder and roughly half of all adults have felt it briefly. It's common; it's just rarely talked about.

how_common.plain: About 1 in 100 people has depersonalization-derealization disorder, and it's more common in teenagers and young adults. Brief episodes are far more common.
how_common.figure: Prevalence about 1% in the general population (2022 systematic review), with earlier estimates of 1–2%; around half of adults have had a brief episode

what_helps.plain_summary: CBT adapted for DPDR is the main treatment: understanding the symptoms, reducing the anxious self-monitoring and avoidance that keep them going, grounding, and gradually re-engaging with life. Treating underlying anxiety, panic, depression, or trauma helps. There's no specific medication for DPDR, though antidepressants prescribed and monitored by a doctor may help co-occurring conditions. Avoiding cannabis is important, as it's a common trigger.
evidence_based_options: Treatment of underlying anxiety, panic, depression, or PTSD
self_help_that_supports_care: Stopping the constant checking of whether you feel real
Grounding through the senses: cold water, textures, movement
Carrying on with normal activities even while feeling unreal
Sleep, and less caffeine and cannabis

when_to_reach_out: If feeling detached or unreal is persistent, distressing, or stopping you living normally, talk to a doctor or therapist and name it; it's often missed. If you start to feel that things actually aren't real, or you have thoughts of ending your life, reach out now.
is_not: Brief unreality during panic, exhaustion, or after cannabis isn't the disorder. In psychosis, the person believes the altered experience is real. Seizures and some medical conditions can cause similar feelings and are ruled out by a doctor.
hope_note: DPDR lifts. People who've felt behind glass for years describe the moment the world came back into colour.

in_young_people: DPDR often starts in the teens, frequently after a panic attack, a period of stress, or cannabis. Teens rarely have words for it and often fear they're going mad; reassurance and naming it help enormously.
